2 0 2 5 - 2 6 The SIP Mindset    Systematic. Intentional. Patient.
SIP isn’t a Sprint. It is a Marathon.
=== page 3 ===
An SIP is not a transaction. It is a declaration that you believe 
in the compounding power of showing up, again and again, in 
the face of uncertainty, distraction, and the temptation to stop. 
The greatest things in the world are never built in a burst. 
They are built in installments.
A soldier does not become battle-ready the moment he 
puts on his uniform. He earns it through countless cold mornings 
of training. A surgeon's hands do not steady themselves in the 
operation theatre. They are trained through years of quiet, 
repeated practice. An orchestra performs as one because every 
individual listens as much as they play.This is the spirit of SIP. 
Systematic, because randomness erodes. Intentional, because every step must mean something. 
Patient, because compounding rewards those who wait.
This Annual Report is not a victory lap. It is a testament to the 
process, to the unglamorous, disciplined, deeply purposeful 
act of preparation. At Edelweiss, we don't just manage wealth. 
We practice endurance. We keep at it.
Every section of this report is framed through a different 
human expression of endurance, drawn from worlds that have 
nothing to do with ﬁnance, yet everything to do with how 
lasting things are made.Index

=== page 8 ===
Our Guiding
Principles 
The Foundations 
We Build Upon
At Edelweiss, our guiding principles are lived before 
they are spoken. They influence the questions we ask, 
the decisions we make, and the standards we uphold. 
Over time, through choices made consistently and with 
intention, they have become part of our institutional 
instinct, guiding actions across teams, businesses, and 
leadership. We strive to be ethical, transparent, and customer-centric in all our dealings, always putting our 
stakeholders' interests first. They encourage us to act 
with integrity, think with empathy, and create with 
accountability. In a world shaped by constant change, 
these principles help us remain patient in our purpose 
and steadfast in our responsibilities.
We are a thinking organisation. We constantly 
bring thought to everything we do. Our clients' 
and our own success depend on our ability to 
use greater ideation and more imagination in 
our approach.We operate as a partnership, internally and 
externally. Though individuals are often brilliant, 
we believe teamwork and collaboration always 
ensure a better and more balanced organisation. 
We also treat our clients as partners and extend 
them the same respect and consideration as our 
internal team members.
We are fair to our clients, our 
employees, and all stakeholders.
We focus on the long-term. As the world is 
poised on the threshold of change and may not 
hold up our assumptions for the future in the 
coming years, we reflect on the long-term 
implications of our actions. Even short-term 
decisions are made with an awareness of 
long-term implications.Our customer experience defines us. 
We strive to make it outstanding every time.
We listen and fulfil the customers’ needs.  
Listening is the start of the relationship with our 
customers wherein we understand their needs 
and fulfil these with the most appropriate 
products and solutions.
We satisfy the needs of all stakeholders. 
Shareholders who entrust us with their capital, 
employees who create the organisation, 
customers who are the reason we exist, and 
society which gives us the resources and 
opportunity to create value.Our financial capital is a critical resource 
for growth. We endeavour to grow, protect, 
and use our financial capital wisely.We focus on growth for our clients, employees, 
and shareholders.
We obey and comply with the rules of the land.  
We maintain the highest standard of integrity and
honesty. When we are unclear, we seek 
clarification from experts. 
We take care of our people. Our policies — in 
letter and in spirit — ensure transparency and 
equal opportunity for all. We go beyond the 
normal goals of attracting, recruiting, retaining, 
and rewarding fine talent. We ensure that every 
individual in Edelweiss has an opportunity to 
achieve their fullest potential.
We respect risk. Our business presents a 
constant challenge of balancing risk and reward. 
Our ability to continually keep an eye on risk 
guides us through this fine balance.Our reputation and image are more important 
than any financial reward. Reputation is hard to 
build and even harder to rebuild. It is impacted by 
our ability to think for our clients, maintain 
confidentiality and by adherence to our ethical 
value system.

Our Governance
Good governance is the surgeon's discipline. 
Every incision, intentional.
Every surgery begins long before the first incision. 
It starts with preparation, discipline, and trust in 
the process. Every step follows a protocol, with 
accountability guiding every decision and long-term 
wellbeing taking precedence over speed. At Edelweiss, 
governance works the same way. It is rooted in 
discipline, accountability, and thoughtful oversight, 
providing the foundation for everything that follows.

Our 
Governance
Built on Responsible Stewardship
At Edelweiss, governance is fundamental to who we are 
and how we operate. It guides our choices, informs our 
conduct, and provides the discipline needed to pursue 
growth responsibly.
Our governance framework is aligned with applicable 
national and global laws and regulations, outlining clear 
and comprehensive guidelines that promote high 
standards of professionalism and ethical conduct 
across the organisation. We enable independent functioning in our businesses, while maintaining 
seamless interdependence. Through our Boards, 
Councils and various operating review mechanisms, 
we continue to stay focused to ensuring good 
governance. More than a set of policies, governance 
represents a shared commitment to ethical conduct 
and principled leadership, enabling us to build 
enduring relationships and sustainable value for 
all our stakeholders.
Tenets of our Corporate Governance PhilosophyKey Highlights
To know more about our Corporate Governance initiatives, please refer to our Sustainability Report.7-member Board of Directors comprising 
4 independent directors, 2 women directors, 
collectively represent ~265 years of rich and 
diverse experience.
Edelweiss Code of Conduct is designed to sensitise 
all employees about our philosophy, values, culture 
and practices. The Code sets out an ethical 
roadmap for the conduct of business.
Senior management and directors are governed 
by conflict-of-interest policy, in addition to the 
Code of Conduct. 
Anti-Bribery and Corruption, Gifts, and 
Entertainment policy safeguards and promotes 
legitimate business.
We endeavour to preserve the confidentiality of 
unpublished price sensitive information to prevent 
any misuse.
'Eleven-risk framework' is institutionalised to 
assess, avoid, manage, and mitigate risks across 
businesses in a continual manner, along with 
Board-level oversight.Our subsidiaries are decentralised, with independent 
compliance officers, following a strong culture of 
compliance, regulatory standards, and remediation 
of escalations.
Major subsidiaries have independent directors who 
ensure keen external oversight and transparency.
Regulatory compliance is automated through 
technology-based applications.
Regular policy refresher workshops and e-learning 
modules are conducted for employees to ensure 
awareness, assimilation, and adherence.
EFSL is ISO 27701:2019 certified and has 
implemented cloud security framework and 
state-of-the-art security solutions for data 
classification, data protection, data loss prevention, 
advanced threat protection, zero-day protection, etc.

Alternative Asset Management business introduced 
online Transfer and Pledge modules for investors, 
enabling seamless completion of transactions 
without manual intervention.
Ellie, an AI tool, was introduced by the Mutual Fund 
business on its website, enabling users to search 
for information, understand financial concepts and 
resolve queries. The business also built dedicated 
microsites for SIF and GIFT offerings to drive 
awareness and investor education.
The NBFC business launched a redesigned website 
and customer portal to enable intuitive self-service 
and faster omnichannel query resolution.Cut the Carbon: Zuno's initiative made insurance 
more seamless and responsible, combining 
paperless processes, digital policy issuance, and 
sustainability-driven actions to offer a convenient, 
purpose-led engagement.In the NBFC business, simplification across the 
onboarding, servicing, and grievance redressal, 
supported by stronger complaint management 
and employee training, improved responsiveness, 
governance and service consistency, resulting in a 
sustained Net Promoter Score (NPS) of 81%, higher 
customer satisfaction, reduced complaints and

Every year, I begin this letter reflecting on the world around us. This year, I want to begin closer to home – with 
Edelweiss itself.
FY26 was a year of two halves: strategically strong but financially flat. Much of the year went into sowing. 
The harvest will show up in the years ahead. 
Symbolically, this is really how Edelweiss has been built – systematically sowing, intentionally tending, and patiently 
waiting for the harvest. Our progress has rarely been defined by a single event. It has come from a steady rhythm of 
purposeful actions – each one building on the last and compounding over time. 
This is what I call the SIP mindset: Systematic, Intentional, Patient. It is a mindset I will return to later in this letter, 
one that, as it turns out, our own shareholders have been quietly teaching us for years, month after month, in the 
form of a habit most of us take for granted: the SIP.
To understand the work we have been putting in and the compounding we expect in the years ahead, let's first look 
at FY26 through the strategic milestones that defined the year.Letter Chairman’s
Rashesh Shah

FY26 - The Year That Was
WestBridge Capital came in as a strategic partner in our Mutual Fund business, acquiring a 15% stake in the 
business. The transaction brought in a seasoned, high-quality and long-term institutional partner, as Edelweiss

with SEBI in January and received approval soon after. In March, we placed 4.4% of EAAA's common equity – while 
our original intent was to place around 4%, we had very strong demand and subsequently increased the placement, 
restricting it to 4.4%. The allocation went to key LPs and select individual investors who have been long-standing

Reﬂections Over The Years
Looking back, the last few years offer me one connected lesson.
As Edelweiss grew, our capital became increasingly concentrated in credit businesses. That capital intensity brought 
higher borrowings with it. And when the shocks arrived – first IL&FS, then COVID – the combination of capital 
concentration, leverage and structural complexity took away much of our room to manoeuvre. The reset, I realised, 
could not just be financial. It had to be architectural.
The story of the last few years at Edelweiss has really been the story of that architectural reset: rebalancing 
capital, reducing debt, simplifying the institution, and building businesses that can compound with more 
discipline and less drag.
Asset-light, capital-efficient models deliver higher returns. In FY26, our Asset Management platforms – Alternative 
Asset Management and Mutual Fund – generated an RoE of around 28%, while Credit (Asset Reconstruction, NBFC 
and Housing Finance) generated around 6%. That gap tells its own story. Credit remains important to us. But credit 
is capital-hungry by design – every rupee of growth needs a rupee of balance sheet behind it. Asset Management 
compounds on people, innovation and execution; Credit compounds on capital. For a long time, we were tilted too 
heavily towards Credit. Correcting that imbalance has been the work of the last few years.The shift is visible in the numbers. In FY16, Credit 
contributed 82% of our Ex-insurance Operating 
Business PAT, with Asset Management contributing 
18%. By FY26, Credit's share had come down to 
52%, and Asset Management's had risen to 48%.But the net worth mix tells you the other, less flattering 
half of the story. Credit still accounts for 82% of 
Ex-insurance Operating Business Net Worth in FY26, 
against 18% for Asset Management. The imbalance 
has reduced. It has not disappeared.

Capital concentration and high borrowings were never really two separate problems. They were symptoms of one 
larger, architectural problem. By 2016, Edelweiss had become a diversified financial services conglomerate, but also 
a genuinely complex one: a monolithic, balance-sheet-heavy structure with significant P&L concentration in Credit. 
In that structure, capital did not move easily between businesses, individual businesses were rarely valued on their 
own merit, and the whole thing was harder to understand from the outside than it should have been. We needed to 
pivot, and the pivot had to go beyond the financials, into the architecture itself. IL&FS and then COVID accelerated 
that reset. By 2021, we were underway: moving from a capital-heavy, integrated structure towards a simpler, 
asset-light institution built around independent, monoline businesses.

From 2020 onwards, we simplified deliberately, in stages. First, we separated operations. Then, we built 
independent management teams under board-led governance. Finally, we separated infrastructure – offices, 
technology platforms, business-specific domains, financial systems. None of this was simplification for its own sake; 
it was meant to improve accountability, make value creation easier, reduce contamination risk between businesses, 
and let investors judge each business on its own merits.
"Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication." 
 - Leonardo da VinciThe number that captures it best: our entity count has come down from 67 to 29.

The result, I believe, is a leaner and more agile Edelweiss — a portfolio of independent, high-growth businesses, 
each creating and unlocking its own value, held together by a lean centre that provides governance and strategic 
oversight, rather than a heavy one that gets in the way.
This, to me, is the larger reflection of the last few years. Where capital sits affects leverage. Leverage affects 
resilience. Architecture affects accountability, valuation and the choices you can make when things get hard. 
Architecture, in other words, is strategy.
Looking back, not every choice we made looks perfect in hindsight, but the underlying businesses have always 
been good ones, and good businesses, given time, capital discipline and the right architecture around them, 
keep creating value.
"Mistakes fade away; winners can forever blossom." 
 - Warren Buffett
For winners to blossom, patience matters as much as the climate around them – and I said earlier in this letter that 
I would return to the idea of patient compounding. This is where I want to draw it out fully, because it turns out to 
be a lesson I have learned, more slowly and more personally, in almost every other part of my life too. Simple is rare. Simple is genius. Annual Report

That consistency is what 
makes the SIP powerful.The SIP Mindset 
Let me come now to the metaphor on the cover of this year's report, because I want to spend a moment on it.
I have used metaphors in these letters before, and most of them have been borrowed — from the arts, from cinema, 
from literature. This year's metaphor is, finally, one borrowed from our own shareholders – from the millions of 
ordinary Indian households who have been showing us, every month, for years, what compounding actually looks 
like in practice.
A Systematic Investment Plan is the simplest financial instrument in this country. It took investing – something that 
once felt large, distant and intimidating – and broke it into small, accessible, repeatable units. In many ways, it 
sachetised investing. Every month, on the same day, a fixed amount moves from a household's bank account into 
a fund. It could be as little as `100 or much more. The amount matters less than the habit – that is the real genius of 
the SIP. It does not just sachetise a financial instrument; it sachetises a habit. It turns investing from an event into a 
rhythm. The contribution happens regardless of conditions. Markets up. Markets down. News good. News bad. 
Bull years. Bear years. The contribution happens.The same is true of relationships. Some of the most consequential compounding decisions of my life were made 
long before I understood they would compound. Vidya and I met as classmates at IIM Ahmedabad in  1987. 
Long walks across campus, working through an M&A research project together, became the seedbed of more 
than three and a half decades of partnership that has been built one ordinary conversation at a time.
Our children, Neel and Avanti, are now adults pursuing their own paths. The compounding of presence in a parent's 
life cannot be accelerated, and the time we did not invest then is not recoverable now. This is the SIP lesson I have 
learned most painfully – and, in time, most usefully.
The same idea extends beyond the personal. Some investments compound not in our own lives, but in the lives of 
others. Philanthropy is one such investment. EdelGive was founded by Vidya in 2007, after she stepped down as 
Edelweiss' CFO. The thesis was simple: bring the same discipline we use to build a financial services business to 
the work of building grassroots non-profits. Eighteen years later, EdelGive has worked with over 150 small and 
mid-sized NGOs across India, providing capacity-building support that often matters more than the cheque itself. 
Philanthropy is the purest SIP I know – the returns don't show up in any quarter, any year, or sometimes any decade. 
They show up in the lives of people you may never meet. Some of the strongest NGOs EdelGive works with were 
started by founders twenty or thirty years ago, when nobody was watching. They did not announce a vision and then 
build it. They simply showed up every day and let the vision emerge.
Progress comes not from occasional intensity but from consistent effort, wise energy management, and the 
discipline to keep showing up. I am increasingly convinced the same is true of building a life. And, of course, 
it works just as powerfully in building institutions and scaling businesses. "The first rule of compounding: never interrupt it unnecessarily." 
- Charlie Munger
The mathematics is familiar. The lesson is deeper. To me, that is the essence of the SIP mindset – a philosophy of 
disciplined compounding; the habit of showing up, making deliberate choices, and giving those choices enough 
time to work.
The idea of an SIP is bigger than finance. The same discipline that builds a portfolio over twenty years builds 
everything else worth building over a lifetime – health, relationships, philanthropy, and, as I will come to, institutions 
like Edelweiss itself. Small, consistent investments, made quietly over time, compound in ways you rarely notice 
while they're happening.Take a simple SIP of
₹ 10,000 a month.
At 12% annual returnsAn investor puts in `12 lakh over 10 years, 
and the corpus grows to about

Race day is just a moment. Endurance training has reinforced this most simply for 
me. The race day is one morning of one weekend in one year. The real value lives in the 
discipline, the preparation, and the strange, quiet joy of the daily rhythm — 
the early-morning runs, the long Sunday cycles, the kilometres logged when nobody 
is watching and there is no medal at the end. 
SIP beyond wealth. Due to health reasons, I was kept away from sports for most of my early years. I came back to it as an adult – first 
tennis, then running, then triathlon after a tendonitis injury paused my running in 2013. Across all three, I have 
learned more about pacing from endurance sport than from any business book. Health is the slowest-compounding 
asset most of us own. It takes decades to build and can be undone in a quarter. As with any SIP, the contribution 
that matters most is the one made on the day you don't feel like making it.Annual Report

Underneath all of this, though, there is a slower, steadier story unfolding 
– one I find more important than any quarter's headline, and one that 
speaks directly to why I believe in India's and Edelweiss' future.The World Around Us
India's growth story remains structurally sound – supported by domestic demand, financialisation, formalisation and 
rising household wealth. The RBI has projected India's growth at around 6.6% for FY27, which keeps us among the 
fastest-growing major economies even as global growth stays under pressure.
The world, though, reminded us again this year how quickly calm can turn fragile. Before the recent de-escalation, 
the disruption around the Strait of Hormuz had pushed up oil-supply concerns, added pressure on the rupee, 
and stoked worries about imported inflation, the current account and corporate margins. By July 2026, FPIs had 
reportedly sold around `2.5 trillion of Indian equities. Developments around the Strait continue to influence 
energy-supply risks and oil prices, with important implications for India's inflation, current account and rupee 
stability. Shipping and trade flows remain sensitive to the evolving geopolitical environment, which continues 
to be fluid. If there is one thing I would want us to take from this, it is that macro shocks can turn quickly, and 
businesses have to be built with buffers, not just forecasts.Edelweiss has been built the same way – steadily, patiently. Nuvama was built over 18 years and is today India's 
second-largest wealth management platform. EAAA has been built over 15 years and is now a large, high-quality 
alternatives platform managing an AUM of ~`73,000 crore – a 70-fold increase since inception. Our Mutual Fund 
business, which began in 2008, has grown into a platform with `1.58 trillion of AUM, including `78,000 crore of 
equity AUM in FY26. None of it was built overnight. It came from staying with the opportunity, improving year 
after year, and letting disciplined effort compound.The SIP mindset shows up in our numbers, but it shows up even more in our people. Businesses compound when 
people compound, when teams learn together, make better decisions, build trust, and stay with difficult problems 
long enough to actually solve them. At Edelweiss, the average tenure of our senior management team is around nine 
years. That continuity matters, as it gives us memory, judgement and patience – the things you actually need to build 
something steadily and build it well.
That is the mindset we bring to building Edelweiss. But no business compounds in a vacuum, and the climate 
around us today is one of contrasts – a resilient India, a still-fragile world, and an Indian household story that is 
quietly reshaping the opportunity in front of financial services. Let me turn to that.` CrCompounding leaders, not just businesses. Annual Report

In the last decade, India has witnessed the 'Financialisation' of household assets as we transitioned from a country 
of savers to investors. Within financial assets, the share of deposits and cash have gone down giving way to the rise 
of the equity segment. The fastest growth over the last decade has come from products that demand disciplined, 
long-term investing — most notably mutual funds and alternative investments, which have emerged as the fastest-
growing segments.Equity includes direct equity holdings by individuals and individual investments in equity mutual funds. 
Others category includes AIFs, Bonds, EPF and NPS.
The next layer of the story is, to me, the more interesting one. At the current household assets to GDP ratio of 4–5x, 
an India that grows into a $10 trillion economy by 2035 would see its household asset pool expand to $40-50 trillion. 
More importantly, in the next decade, the Indian household balance sheet is poised to witness a structural reversal 
with financial assets overtaking the physical assets. To put this in perspective, in the next decade, India could add 
more in financial assets alone (~$16 trillion) than the entire household assets in 2025!Indian households today hold an estimated $16 trillion in assets. India is still, at heart, a "physical assets first" 
economy. Household wealth is still predominantly held in the traditional stores of value – homes, land, gold – that 
families have relied on for generations, while financial assets remain a smaller part of the household balance sheet. 
But that is beginning to shift. Physical assets still account for roughly 60% of household wealth, but that share has 
been gradually declining over the last decade as financial assets – mutual funds, direct equities, alternatives and 
other market-linked products – steadily gain ground, helped by rising financial literacy, wider access to digital 
platforms, a broader product suite, and a growing preference for market-linked returns.Annual Report

Put together, this is really three shifts moving in the same direction: from physical assets to financial assets; within 
financial assets, from saving to investing; and within investing itself, a steady move up the risk-return curve, taking 
Indian households progressively beyond traditional instruments. 
Each of these shifts is creating its own set of needs – households looking to monetise the real estate and gold sitting 
idle on their balance sheets; promoters and family offices, whose wealth has grown manifold over two decades, 
looking to diversify beyond concentrated core equity into uncorrelated, high-alpha assets; retail investors wanting 
income-oriented solutions that offer stable cash flows through volatile markets; and, as India ages, a growing need 
for secure, reliable income through retirement.
For Edelweiss, this is a long-term tailwind. Our Credit platforms help households unlock value from physical assets; 
our Alternatives and Mutual Fund platforms serve promoters, family offices and retail investors as they diversify and 
move up the risk-return curve; and our Life Insurance business addresses the enduring need for protection, income 
and retirement security. Taken together, we sit across almost the entire pipeline of this transition – helping Indian 
households move from simply owning assets to building diversified, long-term financial wealth. As that journey 
gathers pace, trust and performance will matter more than ever, and that is exactly where I believe Edelweiss 
has a role to play, true to what we have always said: Ideas Create, Values Protect.
Looking Forward - Plans for FY 27
Four things will define the year ahead for us.
The Edelweiss Alternatives listing will be the second public-market valuation marker for one of our businesses. 
The Mutual Fund business will continue to scale, anchored by strong Equity AUM growth – the business has 
reached a stage where operating leverage, an improving product mix and rising SIP flows can start to create a 
compounding effect of their own. Both Insurance businesses should reach break-even in FY27, a genuine 
milestone after years of investment, after which our consolidated profitability will finally reflect the full operating 
capacity of the group, without carrying the start-up burn of two subsidiaries. Our Credit businesses will keep 
scaling, but in a more capital-efficient way, with continued emphasis on improving RoE while holding onto balance 
sheet strength and underwriting discipline. 
And we will keep simplifying, leaning into asset-light businesses that compound with less capital, and deleveraging 
along the way. It is what positions us for the decade of household compounding I described earlier - a simpler, 
lighter Edelweiss, built to grow alongside the Indian household.
In Closing
Let me close with two things that matter deeply in any long compounding journey: gratitude and accountability.
To my colleagues across our seven businesses – more than 6,000 of you, serving 14 million customers across this 
remarkable country – thank you, simply, for being the reason any of this is possible.
To our independent directors, who hold us to the highest levels of governance and challenge us to grow and 
innovate, thank you for the rigour and the candour that make us better.
To our partners, regulators, and the broader ecosystem within which we operate – thank you for the trust that 
lets us do what we do.
And to you, our shareholders – thank you, as always, for the patience that has let Edelweiss be built the way 
Edelweiss needed to be built.
The next time I write to you, I will report against the EAAA listing, the insurance break-even commitments, and value 
creation across businesses. 
As Warren Buffett once wrote, "combining savings with compound interest works wonders." That is the spirit 
in which Edelweiss has been built – patiently, deliberately, over time. It is the spirit in which we will keep 
building.
Yours sincerely,

Responsible Investment 
Responsible investing is integral to how we operate. 
We are among the few Indian alternative asset managers 
to have signed the United Nations-supported Principles 
for Responsible Investment, with our commitment dating 
back to January 2023; our first mandatory UNPRI 
report for FY24-25 is completed with the report and 
assessment score available on the UN PRI website. 
Our ESG Policy is aligned with the PRI and guided by 
the ten principles of the UN Global Compact. Vintage 
Special Situations Funds are classified as Article 8 funds under the EU Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation, 
with periodic reporting on the environmental and social 
characteristics they promote.
ESG governance is anchored by an ESG Governing 
Council comprising senior leaders from Edelweiss 
and EAAA Alternatives, which provides strategic 
direction and ensures effective monitoring and 
stakeholder reporting.
EAAA Alternatives became a signatory to the United 
Nations-Supported Principles for Responsible 
Investment (PRI) in January 2023. We have been publishing comprehensive 
Sustainability Reports since FY20 which showcase 
our performance against adopted benchmarks and

standards. Our latest ESG report for FY24-25 was

and advisory partner to funders, including individuals, 
HNIs, corporates, institutions, and foundations, both 
international and domestic, with a specialisation in 
multi-stakeholder collaboration. Through a unique

This sequencing ensures that organisational stability is 
established prior to expansion, creating the conditions 
necessary for sustained engagement and meaningful 
cross-landscape learning. The GROW+ programme 
thwas formally launched in Jodhpur on 7  August 2025. 
The convening brought together over 100 participants, 
including anchor organisations, programme partners, 
ecosystem actors, philanthropic institutions, and 
government representatives, to discuss the evolution of 
the GROW Fund and its next phase. It underscored a 
shared responsibility among stakeholders to continue 
supporting community-led solutions, positioning 
GROW+ as a platform for facilitating the flow of 
resources, expertise, and collaborative networks to 
grassroots organisations.
Participants affirmed that achieving long-term outcomes 
requires a shift from transactional engagements to 
partnerships grounded in mutual respect and a shared 
vision, as well as the role of unrestricted funding and 
capacity-building in enabling organisations to 
strengthen internal systems, build leadership pipelines, 
and adopt more adaptive operational strategies.
With PHIA and GRAVIS onboarded as the first two 
Anchor organisations, the subsequent phase focused 
on the shortlisting, reviewing, and onboarding of partner 
organisations across two distinct landscapes: the Indian 
Desert and the Peninsular Plateau. Drawing on their extensive grassroots presence and 
contextual understanding, the Anchors played a central 
role in identifying, screening, and recommending 
potential partner organisations. The Review Committee 
conducted an independent assessment and provided 
final validation, resulting in the selection of 34.
To formalise engagement across these pyramids,
the first All Partners Convening of GROW+ was held
thin Ranchi on 12  February 2026 in collaboration 
with GRAVIS and PHIA, marking the formal initiation
of programme activities across their 
respective landscapes. 
This convening marked a key structural milestone, 
bringing together all 34 partner organisations to align on 
a shared understanding that climate change is no longer 
an environmental overlay but a cross-cutting force 
shaping livelihoods, migration, governance, soil health, 
biodiversity, and institutional stability. Participants 
shared organisational realities, drawing attention to 
systems operating under increasing pressure.
The pyramid architecture was further validated as a 
model that connects Anchor institutions (GRAVIS and 
PHIA Foundation) with grassroots partners within 
defined landscapes, enabling structured support and 
engagement. Cross-landscape learning emerged as a 
tangible outcome of the convening, as partners from 
PHIA's landscape engaged with GRAVIS teams to 
seek practical guidance on anticipating and managing 
drought-like conditions. This exchange reflected a 
broader shift from geographically isolated 
problem-solving towards a shared understanding 
of climate stress and collective learning. 
The GROW (Grassroots, Resilience, Ownership, and Wellness) Fund: 
GROW was initiated in 2021 in response to the 
institutional fragility observed across organisations in 
the aftermath of COVID-19. The experience 
underscored a key insight: when organisations invest in 
strengthening their internal systems, including human 
resources, financial management, and technology, they 
are better positioned to operate with stability in 
increasingly uncertain environments. 
GROW+ builds on these learnings through a structured 
model that connects Anchor organisations with 
grassroots organisations across distinct landscapes, 
enabling the exchange of knowledge, practices, and 
contextual insights beyond hierarchical flows. 
While continuing to invest in sector-wide capacity 
strengthening as a core strategic priority, the 
programme is designed as a climate-intelligent model 
that supports grassroots organisations in strengthening 
institutional resilience, interpreting evolving climate 
realities, and enabling community-led responses to 
climate challenges. 
At its core, GROW+ seeks to bridge the gap between 
grassroots realities and resource ecosystems by 
ensuring that insights from the ground inform 
institutional strengthening efforts, while also enabling 
more effective communication of systemic needs to 
funders and global actors. 
The programme is structured across two integrated 
yet distinct layers. GROW Classic serves as the 
foundational layer for the first year, focusing on 
establishing institutional readiness through structured 
strengthening across human resources, financial 
systems, technology, and core organisational 
processes. GROW+ builds on this foundation from 
the second year onwards by introducing elements of 
climate intelligence, including access to environmental 
data, cross-country learning networks, evaluation 
frameworks, and global knowledge exchanges 
facilitated through the GROW Global Grid (3G) and 
Climate Fellows.
A session led by Social Lens positioned capacity 
building at the intersection of skills, systems, and 
organisational structures. The discussion clarified the 
distinction between Capacity Building and 
Organisational Development (OD), and the session 
centred on human resources, technology, and financial 
management as critical pillars of institutional 
strengthening. Emphasising the importance of effective 
HR policy, organisational culture, strengthened data 
collection systems, enhanced digital presence, 
budgeting, utilisation tracking, and donor reporting. 
The second half of the convening included a Baithak, a 
closed-door dialogue among partners facilitated by the 
Anchors. This segment was structured as a group 
exercise to explore the social, economic, and political 
contexts of the landscapes, assess changes within 
communities, and map climate risks across organisational 
areas of operation. The convening enabled partners 
across the two landscapes to build connections, deepen 
familiarity, and begin shaping a shared identity as part of a 
collaborative GROW+ network.
A field visit was also conducted in Ranchi, with 
participation from funders, intermediaries, and 
grassroots organisations. 
The visit provided a grounded perspective on 
programme realities in practice. PHIA facilitated the 
visit, with Torpa Rural Development Society for 
Women (TRDSW), a long-standing grassroots partner, 
anchoring field-level engagement. The visit covered 
locations in Bar Toli, Saramoda, and Tunel. Annual Report 
2025-26Edelweiss Financial Services LimitedEdelgive Foundation

The field engagement brought into focus how 
programme design and institutional intent are 
experienced and operationalised at the community

resilience is not built through isolated interventions, 
but through the interplay of strengthened institutions, 
cross-landscape learning, sustained anchor

The interconnectedness of jan, jal, jangal, jameen 
(people, water, forest, and land) emerged as a central

climate action designed from above risks overlooking

the ground are better positioned to generate 
contextually grounded insights that can inform 
broader systems. 
The next phase of GROW+ will focus on transitioning 
from shared diagnosis to coordinated action, while 
avoiding pressures of performative planning or 
extractive reporting. The sequencing will remain 
deliberate, prioritising the strengthening of core 
institutional systems to reduce organisational fragility, 
deepening climate intelligence grounded in lived 
realities, and enabling cross-landscape learning to 
move laterally across the pyramids.

C. Balagopal
Independent DirectorC. Balagopal is the former Chairman (Independent) of the Board of Federal Bank 
Ltd. He is also a Trustee of Anaha Trust; Member of the Governing Council of 
the Centre for Management Development, Trivandrum; Member of the Advisory 
Board of Fourth Wave Foundation; Member of the Board of TIMed Medical 
Devices Incubator of SCTIMST. Balagopal completed his BA and MA from 
Loyola College, Madras University, and joined the IAS in 1977 and worked in 
Manipur and Kerala.
In 1983, he resigned from the IAS to promote a venture to make hi-tech 
biomedical devices for the first time in the country. Acquiring the know-how 
from Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences and Technology, 
Trivandrum (SCTIMST) and with the support of National Research Development 
Corporation and KSIDC, he set up his venture, Penpol Limited, near Trivandrum. In 
1999, Penpol Limited entered into a joint venture with the Terumo Corporation of 
Japan. Today, Terumo Penpol Limited is the biggest manufacturer of blood bags in 
India and one of the world's biggest makers of high-tech biomedical devices. 
In 2012, he sold his stake in Penpol and turned to investing in startups, mentoring 
entrepreneurs, writing (four books to his credit), travel, and his many other 
interests. Balagopal runs a trust, which supports social projects in Kerala and 
Manipur in primary health, primary education, and rural livelihoods. 
Rajiv Jalota
Independent DirectorRajiv Jalota, a former IAS officer with over 35 years of service, has led 
transformational reforms across governance, infrastructure, maritime, industry, 
urban affairs, e-Governance, taxation and public finance. Recognised for 
change management, ease of doing business, and strategic vision, Mr. Jalota 
advanced transparency, efficiency and sustainability in large-scale social and 
economic development, PPPs, public procurement and contract management.
As Chairman, Mumbai Port Authority (as Secretary to Government of India) and 
Indian Ports Association, Mr. Jalota represented India at global maritime 
forums including QUAD, chaired MACN, India steering committee, among 
others. He crafted the Cruise Bharat Mission, CoE on ESG and Circularity, and 
CMEC, and also served as Director General of Shipping. As Additional Chief 
Secretary (Finance), Maharashtra, Mr. Jalota presented a `4 lakh crore 
($58 billion) budget, and as GST Commissioner, Maharashtra, oversaw India's 
largest indirect tax reform in its highest revenue-earning state, winning the 
Prime Minister's Award for Excellence in Public Administration (2017).
He introduced the capital value system of property tax in Mumbai, crafted four 
$4.5 billion civic budgets and planned city-wide solar, water, and sewerage 
systems. As CEO of MIDC, he drove global investor outreach and the creation 
of SEZs and industrial parks through transformative land development and 
PPPs. Mr. Jalota holds a Master's in International Development Policy from 
Duke University and M.Sc. in Chemistry from Lucknow University. Mr. Jalota 
also serves as an Independent Director on the Board of Supreme Industries 
Limited, Dredging Corporation of India Limited, TATA Projects Limited, 
Maharashtra Industrial Township Limited, and NCDEX e-Markets Limited.

A Board Evaluation Policy (the Policy) for evaluating the performance of the Board, its Committees, the Chairman, 
the Managing Director, the Executive Director, the Non-executive Directors and the Independent Directors has been adopted by the Company.
The Policy 
inter alia  provides the criteria for performance evaluation such as Board effectiveness, quality of discussion, 
contribution at the Meetings, business acumen, strategic thinking, time commitment, relationship with the stakeholders, 
corporate governance practices, review of the terms of reference of the Committees and the contribution of the Committees to the Board in discharging its functions, etc.
A separate Meeting of the Committee of the Independent Directors was held wherein the annual performance of the 
Non-Independent Directors, performance of the Board as a whole (including the Committees) and also that of the Chairman, in terms of the provisions of the Act, the Listing Regulations and the Guidance Note issued by SEBI in this regard, was discussed.
INTERNAL FINANCIAL CONTROLS AND RISK MANAGEMENT
The Company has in place adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements. The Company’s internal control system is designed to ensure operational efficiency, protection and conservation of resources, accuracy and promptness in financial reporting and compliance with the laws and regulations. The internal control system is also supported by an internal audit process. The Statutory Auditors and the Internal Auditors of the Company have confirmed that the internal financial control framework is operating efficiently and effectively.
The risk management is an integral part of the Company’s business strategy that seeks to minimise adverse impact on 
business objectives and capitalize on opportunities. The Risk Committee oversees the risk management framework of the Company through regular and proactive intervention by identifying risks and formulating mitigation plans. Further details are provided in the Management Discussion and Analysis Section forming part of this Report.

WHISTLE BLOWER POLICY/ VIGIL MECHANISM
The Company has adopted a Whistle Blower Policy to report genuine concerns/grievances. The Policy is available on the website of the Company at www.edelweissfin.com.

Discussion Management
&Analysis
FY26 unfolded against a backdrop of significant 
geopolitical and economic transition. Beyond the 
normal ebb and flow of economic cycles, the year was 
characterised by structural shifts that continued to 
reshape global trade, investment, and growth patterns. 
The global economy maintained a trajectory of 
moderate expansion despite heightened geopolitical 
tensions, evolving trade corridors, changing 
supply-chain architectures, and shifting capital flows. 
These developments accelerated the reconfiguration 
of economic relationships across regions, creating 
both new opportunities and emerging risks for 
businesses operating in an increasingly interconnected 
world. Growth across advanced economies moderated 
as the cumulative effects of monetary tightening 
weighed on consumption and investment, while 
emerging markets demonstrated relatively stronger 
resilience, supported by domestic demand.
According to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), 
global GDP growth is estimated at 3.0% for 2026. 
While this indicates stable global growth, it also 
underscores a continued divergence between advanced 
and emerging economies. Geopolitical tensions and 
evolving trade patterns remained key sources of 
uncertainty. Energy markets, in particular, experienced 
periodic volatility, with crude oil prices approaching 
$90-100 per barrel during episodes of geopolitical stress. Such volatility continued to pose 
macroeconomic risks, especially for oil-importing 
economies. Global trade growth remained moderate 
amid ongoing supply chain diversification and 
increasing regionalisation of production networks. In this 
environment, economies with strong domestic demand 
and improving infrastructure were better positioned to Macro-Economic Review and Outlook
sustain growth momentum.
Domestic consumption remained the primary driver of 
economic activity, accounting for nearly 60% of GDP, and 
was supported by stable rural demand, normal monsoon 
conditions, and continued urban consumption.
Public investment continued to play a pivotal role in 
supporting economic momentum. Government capital 
expenditure is estimated at `11.2 trillion in FY26, or 
around 3.2% of GDP. Investments in transportation, 
logistics, and energy infrastructure are expected to 
enhance productivity and support long-term growth. Policy initiatives aimed at strengthening domestic 
manufacturing capabilities including Production Linked 
Incentive (PLI) schemes across 14 sectors have further 
supported incremental investments and supply chain 
diversification. The services sector remained the largest 
contributor to economic output, accounting for 52% of 
Gross Value Added (GVA), with financial services, 
technology, and digital platforms continuing to 
expand steadily.
Inflation moderated sharply in the first half of FY26, 
reaching a low of 1.55% in July 2025, driven by 
favourable food prices. It gradually firmed up during 
the second half, ending FY26 at 3.40% in March 2026, 
while remaining within the RBI's 4% target throughout 
the year. The RBI adopted an accommodative monetary 
policy during FY26, reducing the policy repo rate by 
100 bps to 5.25% amid easing inflation and moderating 
growth. System liquidity remained supportive of credit 
expansion, while the banking sector continued to exhibit 
Against this backdrop, India remained one of the 
fastest-growing major economies in FY26 with real 
GDP growth of 7.7% supported by resilient domestic 
demand, sustained public investment, and continued 
strength in the services sector.strong capitalisation and resilient asset quality.
India remained the world's largest recipient of 
remittances, with inflows estimated at approximately 
$135 billion in FY25. Foreign exchange reserves remained 
comfortable at $688 billion during FY26, providing a 
buffer against external shocks. The financial system 
remained stable, with bank credit growth of ~16% YoY in 
FY26 led by services sector, followed by personal loan 
segment, agriculture and allied activities, and industry.
India's economic trajectory continues to be shaped 
by structural shifts that are deepening the financial 
ecosystem and expanding opportunities for the financial 
services sector. Financialisation of household savings is 
gradually accelerating, supporting growth across capital 
markets, asset management, insurance, and retirement 
products. Simultaneously, rapid digitalisation is enhancing 
financial access, efficiency, and customer engagement, 
with Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions India's external sector remained broadly stable 
despite intermittent pressures from global commodity 
price volatility. With around 85% of crude oil 
requirements met through imports, periods of 
elevated oil prices continued to influence the import 
bill. However, this was offset by strong services 
exports and resilient remittance inflows. exceeding 240 billion in FY26. The increasing adoption 
of artificial intelligence and advanced analytics is further 
transforming the sector by enabling personalised 
customer experiences, improving operational efficiency, 
strengthening risk management frameworks, and 
enhancing decision-making capabilities across 
financial institutions.
Continued infrastructure investment and supply chain 
diversification are supporting capital formation across 
sectors such as logistics, renewable energy, and 
manufacturing. Alongside increasing formalisation of the 
economy, these trends are expected to sustain credit 
demand, particularly across retail, MSME, and housing 
finance segments. In parallel, digital platforms, AI-enabled 
analytics, data-driven underwriting, and bank–NBFC 
partnerships are facilitating more efficient credit delivery, 
improving customer acquisition and servicing capabilities, 
and expanding access to financial products across 
India's medium-term outlook remains favourable, 
supported by strong structural fundamentals, policy 
stability, and continued investment momentum. 
According to the International Monetary Fund, India 
is expected to remain the fastest-growing major 
economy globally, with growth projected at 6.4% 
over the medium term.
underserved segments. 
While external risks persist including geopolitical 
developments, commodity price volatility, and global 
financial conditions, India's strong domestic demand 
base and deepening financial ecosystem provide a 
Over the long term, economic progress will be shaped 
not only by cyclical dynamics but by the strength of 
institutions, markets, and policy frameworks that 
channel savings into productive investment. 
solid foundation for sustained growth.
As India's economy continues to formalise and 
deepen, a stronger and more inclusive financial 
ecosystem supported by innovation, entrepreneurship, 
and capital formation will play a critical role in sustaining 
long-term growth.Annual Report

Industry Structure and Developments
Alternative Assets (Private Credit and Real Assets)
India's financial ecosystem is undergoing a structural 
transformation. For decades, household savings were 
synonymous with traditional bank deposits; today, 
we are witnessing a decisive migration towards Mutual 
Funds and Alternative Asset Management. Driven by 
rising financial sophistication, increasing disposable 
incomes, and a robust digital infrastructure, Indian 
investors are aggressively seeking alpha through 
diverse, non-traditional asset classes.
The Indian Alternative Investment Fund (AIF) space 
has matured into three distinct pillars:Within India's Private Alternatives investment landscape, 
over the last decade Real Assets and Private Credit 
have provided investors superior risk-adjusted returns 
leading to development of this market. 
Public Alternatives: Hedge Funds and 
Concentrated Public Equity Mandates.
Private Alternatives: Real Assets (Infrastructure/ 
Real Estate), Private Credit, and Private Equity.
Perpetual Strategies: Yield-generating Vehicles 
such as Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) 
and Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs).By 2030, India is set to become the 
world's third-largest economy with a 
projected GDP of $7.3 trillion. This 
presents a massive $276 billion 
opportunity for Alternative Assets, 
creating an attractive investment 
environment. Within this, Real Assets 
and Private Credit in India are 
expected to reach 51% of the Indian 
Alternatives market by 2030 to $140 
billion, leading the industry's growth.Mutual Funds
India's Mutual Fund industry is making signiﬁcant 
strides, characterised by consistent growth and 
promising indicators. With a strong track record of 
performance and a diverse range of investment options, 
it is well-positioned to meet the needs of various 
investors. In FY26, Mutual Funds Industry AUM grew 
st12%, reaching `73.7 trillion as of 31  March 2026,

Industry Structure and Developments
Alternative Assets (Private Credit and Real Assets)
India's financial ecosystem is undergoing a structural 
transformation. For decades, household savings were 
synonymous with traditional bank deposits; today, 
we are witnessing a decisive migration towards Mutual 
Funds and Alternative Asset Management. Driven by 
rising financial sophistication, increasing disposable 
incomes, and a robust digital infrastructure, Indian 
investors are aggressively seeking alpha through 
diverse, non-traditional asset classes.
The Indian Alternative Investment Fund (AIF) space 
has matured into three distinct pillars:Within India's Private Alternatives investment landscape, 
over the last decade Real Assets and Private Credit 
have provided investors superior risk-adjusted returns 
leading to development of this market. 
Public Alternatives: Hedge Funds and 
Concentrated Public Equity Mandates.
Private Alternatives: Real Assets (Infrastructure/ 
Real Estate), Private Credit, and Private Equity.
Perpetual Strategies: Yield-generating Vehicles 
such as Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) 
and Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs).By 2030, India is set to become the 
world's third-largest economy with a 
projected GDP of $7.3 trillion. This 
presents a massive $276 billion 
opportunity for Alternative Assets, 
creating an attractive investment 
environment. Within this, Real Assets 
and Private Credit in India are 
expected to reach 51% of the Indian 
Alternatives market by 2030 to $140 
billion, leading the industry's growth.Mutual Funds
India's Mutual Fund industry is making signiﬁcant 
strides, characterised by consistent growth and 
promising indicators. With a strong track record of 
performance and a diverse range of investment options, 
it is well-positioned to meet the needs of various 
investors. In FY26, Mutual Funds Industry AUM grew 
st12%, reaching `73.7 trillion as of 31  March 2026, 
stcompared to ` 65.7 trillion as of 31  March 2025. T
his growth is fuelled by a combination of factors, 
including the rising ﬁnancial literacy among the populace, 
favourable performance of the stock market, and the 
convenience of digital investing. Notably, there is a rising 
involvement of young Indians in equity investments, 
driven by the desire to build wealth in a changing 
economic landscape. Technology has played a pivotal 
role in democratising access to mutual funds, offering 
simpliﬁed processes and user-friendly platforms that 
make investing more accessible to a wider audience.
Looking forward, the outlook for India's Mutual Fund 
industry remains promising. With ample opportunities for 
expansion and the potential to attract new investors, the 
industry is poised for further growth. As more participants 
enter the market and innovative products emerge, we 
anticipate an exciting journey of wealth creation and 
ﬁnancial empowerment. While challenges may arise, 
the resilience and adaptability of India's Mutual Fund 
industry position it for continued success in the years 
ahead. With a strong foundation and a commitment to 
innovation, the industry is well-equipped to navigate 
obstacles and capitalise on emerging opportunities, 
driving sustained growth and prosperity for investors.

MSME Finance
The MSME sector remains a key pillar of India's 
economy, contributing meaningfully to GDP, 
manufacturing output, exports, and employment 
generation. With around 9 crore MSMEs registered on 
the Udyam portal, the sector continues to beneﬁt from 
formalisation, technology adoption, and policy support, 
which are expected to further strengthen its role in 
India's growth trajectory over the medium term.
 Despite strong policy support, a large MSME credit 
gap of ` 25–30 trillion persists, creating signiﬁcant 
opportunity for formal lenders, particularly as secured T
he Union Budget 2026–27 
reinforced the Government's 
focus on scaling and 
strengthening MSMEs through 
measures such as the `10,000 
c
rore SME Growth Fund, 
enhanced credit support 
mechanisms, mandatory TReDS 
onboarding for CPSE payments, 
and additional capital infusion 
into MSME-focused funds. MSME lending continues to improve through better 
underwriting, digital data usage, and collateral-backed 
lending structures. 
NBFCs remain integral to this ecosystem, 
complementing banks by addressing niche, 
underserved, and semi-formal MSME segments.
Their agility, regional depth, and customised product 
structures position them well to serve ﬁrst-time 
borrowers, self-employed customers, and small 
enterprises with evolving credit needs. NBFCs have 
also been at the forefront of leveraging digital public 
infrastructure, alternative credit assessment models, 
and co-lending arrangements, enabling faster 
turnaround times and broader ﬁnancial inclusion.
With the RBI having cumulatively reduced policy rates 
since early 2025 and maintaining a stable monetary 
stance, borrowing costs have moderated, supporting 
liquidity conditions for NBFCs. While near-term margin 
pressures persist due to competitive pricing and higher 
funding costs, the overall sector outlook remains stable, 
underpinned by adequate capitalisation, improving 
asset quality, and disciplined growth strategies.Housing Finance 
The Indian housing ﬁnance sector continues to grow 
steadily, supported by resilient housing demand, rising 
urbanisation, and improving mortgage penetration. 
Individual housing loans stood at `37.2 lakh crore 
a
s of September 2025, growing 9.5% YoY, while 
disbursements remained healthy at `4.4 lakh crore in 
H1FY26.
 The housing loan-to-GDP ratio has steadily 
increased over the past decade, though mortgage 
penetration in India still remains below peer economies, 
indicating signiﬁcant long-term growth potential. Housing 
prices have also remained ﬁrm across major cities, 
reﬂecting underlying demand strength.
The operating environment remains supportive, 
aided by government initiatives such as PMAY and
infrastructure-led development in Tier II and III markets. While macroeconomic conditions will continue to 
inﬂuence sector growth, the medium-term outlook 
remains constructive.
Affordable housing, in particular, continues to be a key 
structural growth opportunity driven by urbanisation, 
rising aspirations, and underserved customer segments. 
Affordable Housing Finance Companies are well 
positioned to address this gap through specialised 
underwriting models, deeper regional presence, and 
customer-centric distribution. 
At Nido, affordable housing remains central to our 
strategy, with a strong focus on Tier II and III markets 
through smaller ticket-size lending, doorstep servicing, 
simpliﬁed processes, and analytics-driven underwriting 
aimed at expanding access to formal credit.
Regulatory support through priority sector lending 
norms, along with increasing digitisation, improved 
underwriting capabilities, and better data availability, 
continues to strengthen the reach and efficiency of 
formal housing finance.

General Insurance
The Indian general insurance sector recorded YoY 
growth of 9.3% in FY26, a signiﬁcant increase from 
the 6.2% growth seen in the previous year.
The growth reﬂects a more supportive market 
environment, alongside the industry's continued focus 
on operational efﬁciency, cost discipline, and alignment 
with IRDAI's vision of a transparent and technology-
driven ecosystem. Insurers continued to focus on 
reducing operational inefﬁciencies, maintaining cost 
discipline, and enhancing customer service.
Standalone Health Insurers (SAHI) expanded their 
presence, increasing market share to 13.6% from 
12.5% last year, driven by rising demand for retail health 
products. Public sector general insurers and specialised Private general insurers maintained their leadership 
position with a stable market share of around 52%. PSU insurers experienced a slight decline in their market 
share at 30.5% and 3.5% respectively. 
Motor insurance grew by 9.2% YoY, supported by 
volume growth; however, insurers faced margin 
pressure due to pricing competition and rising repair 
costs. Health insurance reported robust growth of 
15.4%, primarily led by retail demand. At the same time, 
the push for regulatory standardisation added stress to 
underwriting margins and loss ratios. The Fire Insurance 
segment saw a 13.4% increase, supported by volume 
growth affected by premium rate softening and 
increased competitive intensity. Crop insurance, 
despite a degrowth by 27.2%, continued to contribute 
approximately 6.5% of total industry premiums, 
remaining a strategically signiﬁcant line of business 
due to its rural outreach and EOM beneﬁts.
The industry began preparations for adopting Ind AS 
117, the new insurance accounting standard. Insurers 
initiated system alignments and operational updates to 
ensure a smooth transition and regulatory compliance.
The Indian general insurance industry remains 
fundamentally resilient. Regulatory reforms introduced 
during FY26 are expected to enhance governance 
structures, improve customer outcomes, and strengthen 
the sector's long-term sustainability. Continued 
investment in digital infrastructure, innovation, and 
customer-centric practices will be critical in navigating 
future growth opportunities. While global markets continue to contend with 
geopolitical uncertainties, evolving trade dynamics and 
interest-rate volatility, India's structural growth drivers 
remain intact, creating a conducive environment for 
long-term financial services businesses.
Against this backdrop, Edelweiss remains focused on 
executing its strategy of building scalable, diversified, 
and capital-efficient financial-services franchises.
Over the past several years, Edelweiss has 
systematically transformed its business mix, 
strengthened its balance sheet, reduced legacy 
exposures, and invested in building long-duration 
businesses across asset management, credit, and 
insurance businesses. As these investments mature, 
Edelweiss is increasingly positioned to benefit from 
operating leverage, improving profitability and value-
unlocking opportunities.
Edelweiss enters FY27 with strong momentum across 
its diversified businesses, supported by improving 
profitability, operating leverage and disciplined 
execution. The Alternatives platform is expected to 
remain a key growth driver, benefiting from robust fundraising, increasing institutional participation, and 
value-unlocking initiatives, including the proposed EAAA 
IPO. The Mutual Fund business remains well positioned 
for growth, driven by increasing retail participation and 
SIP flows, with continued emphasis on investment 
performance, distribution reach, digital capabilities, and 
product diversification. The Insurance businesses are 
approaching a critical inflection point and are expected 
to achieve breakeven in FY27, supported by continued 
scale-up, improving operating efficiencies, and a 
maturing business franchise. ARC business remains 
focused on optimising capital deployment across 
opportunities with attractive risk-adjusted returns,
while driving recoveries and resolutions to support 
strong profitability and return on equity. MSME and 
Housing Finance businesses are well positioned to 
capitalise on favourable industry dynamics, supported 
by sustained growth in disbursements, expanding 
customer reach, and disciplined risk management. 
Concurrently, Edelweiss remains focused on reducing 
corporate net debt, enhancing capital efficiency and 
unlocking value through strategic monetisation and 
partnership opportunities. These initiatives are expected 
to strengthen earnings quality, improve financial 
flexibility and support long-term shareholder value 
creation.Edelweiss Outlook

remaining a strategically signiﬁcant line of business 
due to its rural outreach and EOM beneﬁts.
The industry began preparations for adopting Ind AS 
117, the new insurance accounting standard. Insurers 
initiated system alignments and operational updates to 
ensure a smooth transition and regulatory compliance.
The Indian general insurance industry remains 
fundamentally resilient. Regulatory reforms introduced 
during FY26 are expected to enhance governance 
structures, improve customer outcomes, and strengthen 
the sector's long-term sustainability. Continued 
investment in digital infrastructure, innovation, and 
customer-centric practices will be critical in navigating 
future growth opportunities. While global markets continue to contend with 
geopolitical uncertainties, evolving trade dynamics and 
interest-rate volatility, India's structural growth drivers 
remain intact, creating a conducive environment for 
long-term financial services businesses.
Against this backdrop, Edelweiss remains focused on 
executing its strategy of building scalable, diversified, 
and capital-efficient financial-services franchises.
Over the past several years, Edelweiss has 
systematically transformed its business mix, 
strengthened its balance sheet, reduced legacy 
exposures, and invested in building long-duration 
businesses across asset management, credit, and 
insurance businesses. As these investments mature, 
Edelweiss is increasingly positioned to benefit from 
operating leverage, improving profitability and value-
unlocking opportunities.
Edelweiss enters FY27 with strong momentum across 
its diversified businesses, supported by improving 
profitability, operating leverage and disciplined 
execution. The Alternatives platform is expected to 
remain a key growth driver, benefiting from robust fundraising, increasing institutional participation, and 
value-unlocking initiatives, including the proposed EAAA 
IPO. The Mutual Fund business remains well positioned 
for growth, driven by increasing retail participation and 
SIP flows, with continued emphasis on investment 
performance, distribution reach, digital capabilities, and 
product diversification. The Insurance businesses are 
approaching a critical inflection point and are expected 
to achieve breakeven in FY27, supported by continued 
scale-up, improving operating efficiencies, and a 
maturing business franchise. ARC business remains 
focused on optimising capital deployment across 
opportunities with attractive risk-adjusted returns,
while driving recoveries and resolutions to support 
strong profitability and return on equity. MSME and 
Housing Finance businesses are well positioned to 
capitalise on favourable industry dynamics, supported 
by sustained growth in disbursements, expanding 
customer reach, and disciplined risk management. 
Concurrently, Edelweiss remains focused on reducing 
corporate net debt, enhancing capital efficiency and 
unlocking value through strategic monetisation and 
partnership opportunities. These initiatives are expected 
to strengthen earnings quality, improve financial 
flexibility and support long-term shareholder value 
creation.Edelweiss Outlook
Opportunities 
The ﬁnancial services industry in FY27 is expected to be shaped by the interplay of structural growth drivers 
including a strengthening investment cycle, continued ﬁnancialisation of savings, digital transformation and cyclical 
factors such as asset quality trends, funding conditions, and evolving regulatory requirements.
India's growth outlook continues to be supported by 
sustained public infrastructure spending, manufacturing 
expansion, energy transition initiatives, and improving 
private sector capital expenditure. Government 
programs aimed at strengthening domestic 
manufacturing and enhancing logistics and 
infrastructure are expected to drive incremental 
investments across the economy. The continued 
expansion of infrastructure, industrial, renewable 
energy, and urban development projects is creating 
signiﬁcant ﬁnancing requirements. This presents opportunities for ﬁnancial institutions across project 
ﬁnance, structured credit, working capital ﬁnancing, 
capital market fundraising, and advisory services. 
The increasing scale and complexity of investment 
projects is also driving demand for alternative 
ﬁnancing solutions, including private credit and 
infrastructure-focused investment vehicles.

and high-net-worth investor base, supported by 
economic growth, rising entrepreneurship, increasing 
ﬁnancialisation of household savings, and greater 
participation in capital markets. Growing ﬁnancial 
wealth is driving demand for a wider range of

solutions. This trend presents signiﬁcant opportunities for wealth managers, asset managers, and ﬁnancial

including portfolio management services, alternative

The increasing adoption of digital technologies, data 
analytics, automation, and artiﬁcial intelligence is 
reshaping the ﬁnancial services landscape. 
Technology-enabled distribution, underwriting, 
servicing, and risk management are enhancing 
operational efﬁciency, improving customer experience, 
and enabling more informed decision-making.The continued evolution of digital ecosystems and 
platform-based engagement models presents 
opportunities for ﬁnancial institutions to expand customer 
reach, improve productivity, reduce operating costs, and 
strengthen risk management capabilities. Institutions that 
effectively leverage technology and data-driven insights are 
well positioned to achieve scalable growth and sustainable 
competitive differentiation.Technology-Led Transformation of Financial Services
Threats
Global macroeconomic uncertainties, including 
shifts in interest rate cycles across major economies, 
geopolitical tensions, trade policy developments, and 
commodity price volatility, may contribute to periods 
of heightened market uncertainty. Such conditions can 
inﬂuence global capital ﬂows, currency movements, 
market liquidity, and investor sentiment across asset 
classes. In an increasingly interconnected ﬁnancial system, prolonged volatility may impact investment 
activity, funding availability and costs, asset valuations, 
and overall risk appetite. These factors could, in turn, 
affect credit demand, capital market activity, and the 
operating environment for ﬁnancial institutions, 
necessitating greater focus on risk management, 
liquidity planning, and capital allocation.Global Financial Market Volatility
Rapid advances in technology continue to transform 
the ﬁnancial services industry, enabling new business 
models, digital distribution channels, and data-driven 
customer engagement. Fintech ﬁrms and 
technology-enabled competitors are increasingly 
leveraging innovation to enhance customer experience, 
improve operating efﬁciency, and expand access to ﬁnancial services. As technology becomes increasingly 
central to customer acquisition, risk management, 
and service delivery, ﬁnancial institutions that are 
unable to adapt to changing customer expectations
or invest effectively in digital capabilities may face 
increased competitive pressures and potential loss
of market share.Technology Disruption and Evolving Competitive LandscapeRegulators globally and in India are increasingly focused 
on strengthening oversight across the ﬁnancial system, 
with greater emphasis on consumer protection, digital 
lending practices, leverage and capital adequacy, and 
governance standards. While these measures enhance 
the resilience and transparency of the ﬁnancial ecosystem, they also raise compliance requirements 
and operational expectations for ﬁnancial institutions. 
As a result, ﬁrms may need to balance growth 
ambitions with stronger risk management frameworks 
and regulatory discipline.Regulatory Tightening
FY26 was a year of strong execution and strategic 
progress for the company. While the reported financials 
reflect the impact of one-time exceptional items, 
including GST-related adjustments and the 
implementation of the new labour code, the underlying 
operating momentum remained steady. 
Across businesses, performance was robust and 
aligned with strategic priorities. The Alternative Asset 
Management business reported a 32% YoY growth in 
FPAUM to `44,710 crore, supported by strong
fund-raising of ` 10,855 crore, up 64% YoY. The Mutual 
Fund business witnessed healthy growth in equity AUM, 
which increased by 25% YoY to 
`78,000 crore, while 
the SIP book expanded by 58% YoY to `623 crore. 
The Asset Reconstruction business delivered recoveries 
of `8,590 crore, with the share of retail assets in capital 
employed rising to 29%. In the MSME segment, 
disbursements tripled YoY to 
`1,051 crore, alongside a 
calibrated reduction in the wholesale book by 30% YoY 
increasing by 8.2% YoY to `1,750 crore, reﬂecting a 
shift towards granular lending.Performance Highlights
The Housing Finance business maintained its growth 
trajectory, with disbursements increasing by 27% YoY 
to `2,171 crore and AUM growing by 16% YoY to 
`4,906 crore. In the Insurance segment, General 
Insurance gross written premium grew by 28% YoY to 
`1,294 crore, with 872,901 policies issued during the 
year, marking a 47% YoY increase. The Life Insurance 
business reported a 6% YoY growth in gross premium 
to 
`2,221 crore, while AUM increased by 11% YoY to 
`10,425 crore. The insurance businesses remain on 
track to achieve breakeven by FY27, with combined 
losses for the year ended March 2026 reducing by 23% 
over the past two years, reﬂecting improving operating 
leverage and scale beneﬁts.
The Company reported a consolidated Profit After Tax 
(PAT) before minority interest of 
`680 crore for FY26, 
reﬂecting resilient underlying performance supported by 
steady operating momentum and disciplined execution. 
Total income for the year increased to ` 10,865 crore, 
compared to 
`9,519 crore in FY25, driven by growth 
across key business segments as well as gains arising 
from strategic stake sale transactions. 
Interest income grew modestly by 2.8% YoY to 
`2,767 
crore in FY26, as against `2,690 crore in FY25, in line 
with the Company's strategic shift towards asset-light 
retail credit models. The insurance businesses 
continued their growth trajectory, with net premium 
income increasing by 8.2% YoY to `2,835 crore in 
FY26 from ` 2,620 crore in FY25, indicating sustained 
business momentum.The Company continued to strengthen its profitability 
while advancing its transformation into a more 
diversified and capital-efficient financial services 
platform. During the year, key strategic milestones 
were achieved, including acquisition of 10% stake by 
WestBridge Capital in the mutual fund business, as 
well as the sale of a 4.4% stake in EAAA, reinforcing 
the strength and growth potential of these franchises.Annual Report

costs declined by 1.8% to 
`2,492 crore from `2,537 
crore in the previous year, supported by effective liability 
management, while other operating expenses remained 
broadly stable, reﬂecting improved operating efﬁciency 
and scalability. During the year, the Company adopted 
a prudent approach towards risk recognition and 
provisioning. Impairments, including changes in 
valuation of credit-impaired loans, increased to `1,700 
crore in FY26 from `507 crore in FY25. This included 
prudent management overlay and conservative 
provisions of ` 1,400 crore recognised in Q3FY26, 
considered on stress-tested scenarios considering 
macroeconomic uncertainties and evolving geopolitical 
conditions, revised cash ﬂows, and cautious asset 
quality assessment.On the balance sheet front, consolidated net debt 
decreased to `10,430 crore as of March 31, 2026, 
from 
`11,170 crore in the previous year. The Company 
maintained adequate liquidity throughout the year, with 
available resources averaging approximately 38% of 
total borrowings. The Company remains focused on 
further optimising its capital structure and reducing 
corporate net debt going forward.
The diluted Earnings Per Share (EPS) improved to 
`7.15 in FY26 from ` 5.81 in FY25, supported by both 
operating performance and value-unlocking initiatives.

`49 as at the end of 
FY26. The Board of Directors has recommended a ﬁnal 
dividend of 
`1.50 per equity share, resulting in a total 
dividend of 
`1.50 per equity share for FY26, subject to 
shareholder approval.

e ensure that an adequate liquidity cushion is 
maintained to take care of all maturing liabilities with a

At the end of FY26, we maintained available liquidity of 
`6,488 crore. This included overnight liquid assets of 
`2,412 crore, high-quality liquid assets of over `3,725 
crore which can be liquidated within a short span (if the 
need arises), and undrawn committed bank credit lines 
of `351 crore.
Over the years, we have demonstrated a strong track 
record of fundraising from both retail and institutional 
lenders. With the help of public issues and our retail borrowing programmes, we have increased the 
proportion of funding through retail sources from 
52% to 63% in the past one year.
On the asset side, we continue to focus on and reorient 
our balance sheet towards retail growth. As wholesale 
recoveries remain slightly slower than anticipated,
we have optimised the tenure and focused on
medium to long-term borrowings. Long-term borrowings 
now stand at 69% of the total debt.
All these steps have ensured that we maintain a positive

Alternative Asset Management
EAAA India Alternatives Limited (EAAA), is one of the 
leading alternatives platforms in India, with an AUM of  
~ `72,700 crore as of March 31, 2026. With over 16 
years of experience, EAAA operates a diversiﬁed,
multi-strategy platform focusing on Real Assets and 
Private Credit among other strategies. We cater to a 
diverse client base of global and domestic institutional 
clients, UHNIs, HNIs, and family ofﬁces.
 Our Fee paying AUM has grown at a CAGR of 25% over 
last 5 years. During the year, we have raised 
`10,855 
crore. This strong business performance helped in the

eal Assets
EAAA's Real Assets strategy invests in infrastructure 
and commercial real estate assets with low counterparty 
risk and long residual tenures. The sub-strategies 
include Infrastructure Yield, Commercial Real Estate 
Yield, Perpetual Capital (InvITs), and Energy Transition. 
Real Assets FPAUM grew YoY by 35% to ` 25,403 crore. 
The maiden Energy Transition Fund completed its ﬁrst 
close in FY26 and the fundraise currently stands at
~ `1700 crore where we onboarded the European 
Investment Bank (EIB) as an anchor investor of the fund. 
Energy Transition Fund offers investors a long-term 
investment vehicle and an opportunity to participate in 
India's sustainable energy transition. The Infrastructure 
and Real Assets Fund (IRAF) also completed it's ﬁnal close with a fundraise of `2,494 crore. The second

closer to full deployment with a marquee deal by 
acquiring ﬁve fully operational Hybrid Annuity Model
